{"id": "28:81/q29", "question": "What recitation rule applies before ٱلْأَرْضَ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:81/q29/p1", "position": "Transferring the vowel before alif-lām does not restore a preceding long-vowel letter or original sukūn.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī says reciters agree that the consonant moves and the madd is omitted despite Arabic alternatives; he adduces 20:21, 82:1, 4:59, 30:50, 10:51, 24:32, 4:58, 72:9, 77:16, 80:24, 6:103, 6:136, 15:3 and 3:139."}]}
{"id": "28:81/q30", "question": "Where was this sūra revealed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:81/q30/p1", "position": "All of al-Qaṣaṣ is Meccan.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī reports this from al-Ḥasan, ʿAṭāʾ and ʿIkrima."}]}
{"id": "28:81/q31", "question": "What was Qarun's standing before his rebellion?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:81/q31/p1", "position": "He was a learned, wealthy Israelite close to Moses who later became arrogant and rebellious.", "reasons": "Thaʿlabī and Baghawī's historians portray him as Israel's most learned man after Moses and Aaron, a fine or leading Torah reciter, handsome, wealthy, and in Baghawī pleasant-voiced; Thaʿlabī says he allied hypocritically with Sāmirī. Ibn ʿAṭiyya places the episode after the sea crossing and says transmitters credited Qarun with preserving and reciting Torah. Biqāʿī says historical reporters place him among Moses' people and very near him."}]}
{"id": "29:16/q01", "question": "How is إبراهيم read and syntactically governed?", "turns_on": "The case reading and, for the accusative, the governing verb; the surrounding sending formula supports the preferred coordination.", "positions": [{"id": "29:16/q01/p1", "position": "In the common accusative reading, it is coordinated with Noah: God also sent Abraham.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj, al-Naḥḥās and al-Kisāʾī supply 'We sent' from 29:14. Al-Kashshāf and al-Nasafī connect it with Abraham's readiness to counsel. Al-Biqāʿī prefers this construction by the later Midian parallel; al-Ālūsī prefers it by 29:36. Al-Rāzī and al-Samīn identify the accusative as common. Al-Bursawī adds an implied command to recall the time of speech. Islahi explicitly describes Abraham as sent as a messenger to call his people, in parallel with Noah."}, {"id": "29:16/q01/p2", "position": "In the accusative, an omitted 'Remember' governs Abraham.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī makes 'when he said' an inclusion apposition since the time contains the event. Al-Biqāʿī says recalling the exemplary forefather comforts the Prophet and instructs his people. Al-Ālūsī permits coordination of stories with different forms."}, {"id": "29:16/q01/p3", "position": "In the nominative reading, an omitted predicate gives 'Among the messengers was Abraham.'", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf names al-Nakhaʿī and Abū Ḥanīfa as readers; Abū Ḥayyān adds Abū Jaʿfar and Ibrāhīm. Al-Samīn makes Abraham the subject. Al-Ālūsī favors this supplied predicate in light of 29:14–15."}, {"id": "29:16/q01/p4", "position": "The accusative Abraham is coordinated with the object pronoun of 'We saved him' in 29:15.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Kisāʾī and al-Samīn allow it. Al-Ālūsī reports Abū al-Baqāʾ and Ibn ʿAṭiyya offering it, but calls it poor."}, {"id": "29:16/q01/p5", "position": "The nominative may instead supply 'among those to be mentioned' or 'among those saved.'", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports both estimates and prefers 'among the messengers' because of the surrounding verses."}]}
{"id": "29:16/q02", "question": "What is the grammatical function of إذ قال?", "turns_on": "Whether idh modifies sending or belongs to an omitted 'remember'; Abū Ḥayyān disputes the appositional object analysis.", "positions": [{"id": "29:16/q02/p1", "position": "It marks the time of God's sending Abraham.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf says he could then counsel through age and knowledge; al-Bayḍāwī says judgment and recognition of truth had matured; al-Nasafī and al-Ālūsī say he was ready to exhort and guide."}, {"id": "29:16/q02/p2", "position": "It is an inclusion apposition to Abraham under an omitted 'Remember.'", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī says the time contains the event; al-Samīn and al-Biqāʿī give the same parse. Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Nasafī allow it with omitted 'remember.' Abū Ḥayyān objects that past-time idh is not a direct object, and al-Ālūsī reports his objection to making its indeclinable temporal form an object or substitution."}, {"id": "29:16/q02/p3", "position": "An implied command asks the audience to remember the time of his speech.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī combines coordination of Abraham with Noah and this implicit recollection."}]}
{"id": "29:16/q03", "question": "When was Abraham sent in relation to his call?", "turns_on": "Whether 'when he said' requires sending to coincide with speech, and whether 29:18 attests an already existing mission.", "positions": [{"id": "29:16/q03/p1", "position": "He was sent when mature enough in age, judgment and knowledge to counsel his people.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī and al-Ālūsī make this the sense of the temporal phrase."}, {"id": "29:16/q03/p2", "position": "He remained a messenger while speaking; sending is a continuing state.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī raises the problem that preaching ordinarily follows sending and compares ongoing messengerhood to standing that lasts until a prince exits his house."}, {"id": "29:16/q03/p3", "position": "He began calling people through divine guidance before formal sending, which happened while he preached.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī offers this as another resolution of the order problem. Al-Ālūsī reports a similar proposal near adulthood but replies that Abraham's words at 29:18, if his, suggest prior sending; al-Saʿdiyya says the verse need not imply formal mission."}]}
{"id": "29:16/q04", "question": "How does Abraham's account connect with Noah's and Quraysh?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "29:16/q04/p1", "position": "It continues Noah's account by introducing another prophet God sent.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā ibn Sallām links it to 29:14; al-Zajjāj supplies the sending verb. Al-Biqāʿī cites the later Midian parallel, and al-Ālūsī joins the stories despite differing sentence forms. Islahi makes the parallel with Noah explicit and calls Abraham's warning timely counsel for his people."}, {"id": "29:16/q04/p2", "position": "It offers Quraysh a parallel and recalls their forefather's rejection of idols.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān make the analogy explicit. Al-Biqāʿī says remembering Abraham comforts the Prophet and instructs his people."}]}
{"id": "29:16/q05", "question": "Who were Abraham's people in this account?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "29:16/q05/p1", "position": "His own people, identified as Nimrod and the idolaters of his city in Babylon.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān mention Nimrod and his idol-worshiping city; al-Bursawī names Babylon and includes Nimrod. {"id": "29:16/q06", "question": "What is reported about Abraham before he called his people?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "29:16/q06/p1", "position": "He grew unusually fast, then went out to call his people.", "reasons": "Ibn Abī Ḥātim reports al-Suddī: each day of growth equaled a week and each week a month."}]}
{"id": "29:16/q07", "question": "What does اعبدوا الله ask Abraham's people to do?", "turns_on": "The command is unpacked as exclusive monotheism, practical obedience or affirmation of God's existence; al-Rāzī explicitly gives alternative readings.", "positions": [{"id": "29:16/q07/p1", "position": "Worship God alone, affirming His oneness instead of idols or intermediaries.", "reasons": "Muqātil and Yaḥyā gloss worship as oneness; Ibn ʿAṭiyya sets the call among Nimrod's idolaters. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says exclusivity is implicit: idolaters worship angels and jinn as intermediaries to God. Kur'an Yolu asks whether idols have divine qualities. Al-Rāzī argues possible beings require a necessary existent, and two necessary beings would be composite through shared and distinguishing attributes; no partner can share God's status. Ibn Kathīr adds sincere worship, provision sought only from God, and thanks to the sole giver. Islahi says avoiding partners specifically concerns worship of God."}, {"id": "29:16/q07/p2", "position": "Obey God by performing His worship and obligations.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās says 'obey'; al-Ṭabarī says to discharge duties. Al-Rāzī includes affirmation of God and rejection of shirk within obligations and prohibitions. Al-Biqāʿī says worship as God directs. Study Quran calls it a summary of appeals in 19:42, 19:48, 21:52, 21:66, 26:69, 26:76, 37:85 and 37:95."}, {"id": "29:16/q07/p3", "position": "Affirm God's existence.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī reports a paired reading: worship affirms God, while piety denies other gods; association with the sovereign is a grave offense."}]}
{"id": "29:16/q08", "question": "What does وَٱتَّقُوهُ ask them to do?", "turns_on": "The explanations specify fear itself, abstention from forbidden deeds, or especially avoidance of shirk.", "positions": [{"id": "29:16/q08/p1", "position": "Fear God and His punishment.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī, Muqātil and Ibn ʿAbbās say fear God. Al-Qurṭubī specifies His punishment and torment; al-Biqāʿī links association with punishment. Ibn Kathīr and Study Quran speak of reverence alongside worship. Islahi explains fear of God as avoiding His wrath."}, {"id": "29:16/q08/p2", "position": "Avoid sins and prohibited acts.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī says to avoid sins while performing duties; al-Rāzī pairs obligations with abstention from prohibitions."}, {"id": "29:16/q08/p3", "position": "Avoid associating anything with God.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says piety denies any other deity because a partner with the sovereign is a grave offense. Al-Biqāʿī, al-Bursawī and al-Ālūsī explicitly link fear to shunning shirk; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls the p

{"id": "29:16/q09", "question": "With what is ذَٰلِكُمْ خَيْرٌ لَّكُمْ compared?", "turns_on": "Whether khayr compares worship with idolatry, all goods, or nothing.", "positions": [{"id": "29:16/q09/p1", "position": "Worship and piety are better than their idolatry, unbelief or current practice.", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Qurṭubī and al-Bursawī contrast idols or unbelief; al-Bayḍāwī and al-Ālūsī name current practice. Al-Bursawī says the comparative accommodates their false belief, though unbelief contains no good. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr glosses khayr as afḍal, 'better or more excellent.' Al-Jishumī and al-Baghawī state the advantage generally; Ibn Kathīr says it earns good and averts evil."}, {"id": "29:16/q09/p2", "position": "Worship and reverent fear are better than everything beneficial.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says better than anything; al-Ālūsī reports comparison with all beneficial things."}, {"id": "29:16/q09/p3", "position": "Khayr can mean simply 'good,' without comparison.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports this alternative alongside both comparative construals."}]}
{"id": "29:16/q10", "question": "Why are worship and piety better for people?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "29:16/q10/p1", "position": "They bring benefit and avert harm in this life and the hereafter.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr says worship, fear, seeking provision from God and thanking the giver bring good and repel evil in both lives. Kur'an Yolu says obedience benefits people; disbelief harms worldly life and prevents salvation in the hereafter."}, {"id": "29:16/q10/p2", "position": "They draw a person near to sovereign God and raise that person's rank.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī argues humans cannot own heaven and earth, so their highest rank is nearness to the sovereign. He cites 96:19 on prostration and two divine sayings about drawing near through obligations and continued worship. An atheist denies the sovereign, while an idolater posits inferior partners; uniqueness, worship and piety yield higher status to one who understands the proofs."}, {"id": "29:16/q10/p3", "position": "Serving God protects human dignity and personality.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu says serving others damages these, whereas worship and obedience to God benefit the worshiper."}]}
{"id": "29:16/q11", "question": "What does إِن كُنتُمْ تَعْلَمُونَ require or imply?", "turns_on": "Whether the condition specifies practical discernment, recognition of God as Lord, or censures their ignorance.", "positions": [{"id": "29:16/q11/p1", "position": "They must discern benefit from harm and good from evil with reasoned insight.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī invokes recognizing good and harm, with 6:72 and 9:41. Al-Zamakhsharī contrasts discernment with blind ignorance; al-Bayḍāwī contrasts knowledge with ignorance. Al-Ālūsī says even any knowledge suffices to recognize the advantage. Al-Jishumī and al-Bursawī speak of understanding and discernment."}, {"id": "29:16/q11/p2", "position": "They must know God is their Lord.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī reports al-Kalbī's gloss."}, {"id": "29:16/q11/p3", "position": "The condition rebukes their actual ignorance.", "reasons": "Muqātil says they do not know; Ibn al-Jawzī says they fail to know good from bad. Al-Biqāʿī argues even animals seek their benefit, so people who miss this are below animals despite claims to reason."}]}
{"id": "29:16/q12", "question": "Whose speech is the following passage?", "turns_on": "Whether the discourse remains Abraham's or interrupts it with an aside.", "positions": [{"id": "29:16/q12/p1", "position": "The verses continue Abraham's speech.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf reports this for the passage through the endpoint it names as 27:56."}, {"id": "29:16/q12/p2", "position": "The verses include an aside about Muhammad and Quraysh within Abraham's story.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf reports this alternative for the same passage."}]}
{"id": "29:16/q13", "question": "How does this call relate to other Qur'anic portrayals of Abraham and prophetic faith?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "29:16/q13/p1", "position": "Islam renews Abraham's creed, which believers are told to follow.", "reasons": "Study Quran says the Qur'an treats Abraham in over two hundred verses and cites 6:161, 2:130, 3:95, 16:123, 2:135 and 3:67 for following and defining faith by his creed."}, {"id": "29:16/q13/p2", "position": "This command summarizes Abraham's longer appeals elsewhere.", "reasons": "Study Quran cites 19:42, 19:48, 21:52, 21:66, 26:69, 26:76, 37:85 and 37:95."}, {"id": "29:16/q13/p3", "position": "Calling people to the one God is a principle shared by all prophets.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu connects it with examining idols' supposed divinity and remembering earlier peoples who called messengers liars."}]}
{"id": "29:17/q01", "question": "What are the awthān worshipped here?", "turns_on": "Whether the terms wathan and ṣanam are synonyms or distinguished by material, bodily form, or the breadth of objects worshipped.", "positions": [{"id": "29:17/q01/p1", "position": "They are idols, images or statues worshipped besides God.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba calls wathan a stone or plaster idol; al-Ṭabarī calls them likenesses, Qatāda statues, and Bursevī manufactured images. Al-Jawharī equates wathan and ṣanam; Biqāʿī reports lexicographers who agree. Qatāda calls them an idol or stone. Abū Ḥātim notes Christian images of Christ and Mary as objects of prostration."}, {"id": "29:17/q01/p2", "position": "A wathan is specifically a carving of wood or stone, unlike a metal ṣanam.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda contrasts wooden or stone awthān with gold, silver or copper aṣnām; Qurtubī transmits a variant assigning plaster or stone to wathan."}, {"id": "29:17/q01/p3", "position": "A wathan is a bodily object set up for worship, unlike a bodiless ṣanam image.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī reports Abū Manṣūr through al-Qazzāz. Ibn ʿArafa instead includes any plaster, stone or similar image; Abū Ḥātim calls a wall image wathan but a stone statue ṣanam, showing the distinction varies."}, {"id": "29:17/q01/p4", "position": "A wathan is a nonhuman stone image, unlike a human shaped ṣanam of wood or metal.", "reasons": "Bursevī reports this distinction from some authorities."}, {"id": "29:17/q01/p5", "position": "Awthān covers any worshipped object, more broadly than aṣnām.", "reasons": "Elmalılı includes stone images, fetishes, standing stones and crosses. Islahi includes shrines among the baseless objects worshipped."}]}
{"id": "29:17/q02", "question": "What does the root of awthān evoke in this rebuke?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "29:17/q02/p1", "position": "Its associated senses of increase, dispersal and weakness expose idols as unfit for divinity.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī traces permutations of وثن through abundance, scattered reports, weakness and fixed immobility, and takes the plural as scattered objects dividing attention."}]}
{"id": "29:17/q03", "question": "How does إنما govern the clause ending in أوثانا?", "turns_on": "Whether mā merely blocks inna or is its relative noun; the actual accusative awthānan bears on that choice.", "positions": [{"id": "29:17/q03/p1", "position": "Mā blocks inna, making innamā one restrictive particle; awthānan is the object of taʿbudūna.", "reasons": "Naḥḥās says inna cannot govern a verb and that mā still blocks it before a noun. ʿAlī ibn ʿĪsā objects that a relative mā would require nominative awthān. Al-Farrāʾ treats innamā as one particle. Jishumī transmits the restrictive analysis."}, {"id": "29:17/q03/p2", "position": "Mā can be relative, yielding nominative awthān as inna's predicate in a hypothetical construction.", "reasons": "Some grammarians allow the relative analysis before a noun. Naḥḥās and Qurtubī allow it outside the Qurʾānic reading, with taʿbudūna the relative clause and an omitted return pronoun; Jishumī also reports the analysis. ʿAlī ibn ʿĪsā rejects applying it to the actual accusative reading."}]}
{"id": "29:17/q04", "question": "What force does calling their objects only awthān have?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "29:17/q04/p1", "position": "It strips their objects of divine standing and confines their worship to mere manufactured idols.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī says restriction reverses the claim to divinity, while plurality signals division and weakness; Ālūsī stresses that statues have no quality beyond manufacture. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the indefinite plural belittles empty claims and sets true worship with God. Biqāʿī contrasts God, without equal or minister, with the idols."}]}

haping."}, {"id": "29:17/q05/p4", "position": "It can mean originating creation, a sense assigned to God.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba cites 7:189; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says divine usage is origination without precedent; al-Rāghib reserves this sense to God."}, {"id": "29:17/q05/p5", "position": "Khalq can mean religion in other verses.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba reads God's khalq in 30:30 as religion, and reports that changing it in 4:119 can mean changing religion or bodily alterations such as castration and slitting ears."}]}
{"id": "29:17/q06", "question": "How is وتخلقون read?", "turns_on": "Vocalization, gemination and an added or elided tāʾ distinguish the transmitted verb forms.", "positions": [{"id": "29:17/q06/p1", "position": "The common reading is the simple form تخلقون, meaning make or fabricate.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī accepts the regional readers' light khāʾ and ḍamma on lām because the authoritative readers agree; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls it the majority reading. Al-Samīn describes it as from خلق. Al-Zajjāj and Qurtubī record a form spelled like the verse."}, {"id": "29:17/q06/p2", "position": "A doubled-lām form from تخلّق or تتخلّق is read, conveying emphatic invention or lying.", "reasons": "Al-Sulamī, Zayd, ʿAlī, Qatāda, ʿAwn, Ibn Abī Laylā, ʿUbāda and Ibn al-Zubayr appear in varying transmitter lists. Ibn Mujāhid says one tāʾ drops from تتخلقون; Ibn Jinnī compares تكذبون. Some allow the basic فعل sense. The reports describe the initial tāʾ as open."}, {"id": "29:17/q06/p3", "position": "An intensive doubled-lām form from خلق is read, suggesting repeated or abundant making or lying.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī and Ālūsī give the intensive implication; al-Nasafī names Abū Ḥudhayfa and al-Sulamī, and Ālūsī reports Zayd ibn ʿAlī, with lying and slander as its sense."}, {"id": "29:17/q06/p4", "position": "The verb is read تختلقون with an added tāʾ.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Sumayfiʿ and Abū al-Mutawakkil are named by Ibn al-Jawzī."}, {"id": "29:17/q06/p5", "position": "A doubled-lām reading also has ḍamma on the initial tāʾ.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn reports this separately from Zayd ibn ʿAlī."}]}
{"id": "29:17/q07", "question": "What does إفكا mean here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "29:17/q07/p1", "position": "It means a lie, falsehood or perversion of truth.", "reasons": "Jishumī calls it a lie; Bursevī calls it the worst kind of lie. Biqāʿī and Ṭabāṭabāʾī trace it to being turned from proper truth, for a statement or deed. Mujāhid gives the same basic sense; Asad renders the phrase literally as creating a lie."}]}
{"id": "29:17/q08", "question": "What are they doing when they 'create falsehood'?", "turns_on": "Whether the falsehood is primarily their spoken divine claims, the manufactured idols themselves, or a sarcastic characterization; some notes combine carving with the claim.", "positions": [{"id": "29:17/q08/p1", "position": "They invent lies by calling idols gods, partners or intercessors.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī specifies spoken claims, while reports from Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid say uttering or making lies; Mujāhid also extends lies beyond idols. Muqātil joins hand manufacture to the claim of divinity, citing 37:96. Al-Kashshāf, al-Bayḍāwī, Bursevī and others mention partners or intercession. Ibn Kathīr reports invented divine names; Elmalılı compares a portrait to a living person and calls worship of an imagined image slander. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the true God is one. Islahi says their claim that God made these objects His partners has no divine statement or proof."}, {"id": "29:17/q08/p2", "position": "They carve or manufacture idols, which are themselves called falsehood.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, Ibn Zayd and Ibn ʿAbbās are variously reported; Wahidī also gives Mujāhid and al-Kalbī. The things are handmade yet falsely called gods; Ibn ʿAbbās explains the name falsehood by this false claim. Yaḥyā cites 37:95 and Muqātil 37:96. Biqāʿī notes that the present tense evokes continual remaking and the inversion of created artifact into creator. Al-Bayḍāwī and Ālūsī describe making them for falsehood, with Ālūsī's lām of outcome rather than intention. Al-Ṭabarī prefers speech fabrication over merely carving; Ibn Kathīr's report says Ibn Jarīr chooses carving, an attribution that differs from the extant Tabari note."}, {"id": "29:17/q08/p3", "position": "The phrase is a sarcastic description of their supposed creating.", "reasons": "Ālūsī reports this as a further possibility without specifying its target beyond the phrase."}]}
{"id": "29:17/q09", "question": "How is إفكا analyzed grammatically and read?", "turns_on": "Whether the form is a verbal noun, an adjective, or a shortened participle, and whether the initial hamza is read with fatḥa.", "positions": [{"id": "29:17/q09/p1", "position": "The written ifkan is a verbal noun meaning lying or a false act.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf compares kadhib and laʿib. {"id": "29:17/q13", "question": "Why is رزقا indefinite while الرزق is definite?", "turns_on": "Whether the article expresses totality, known promised provision, or deliberate repetition beyond the usual definite noun rule.", "positions": [{"id": "29:17/q13/p1", "position": "Negated indefinite رزقا excludes even the least provision; definite الرزق encompasses all provision from God.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf, cited also by Rāzī, states the contrast; Bayḍāwī says the indefinite is general. {"id": "29:17/q16", "question": "What does the command to worship God require and accomplish?", "turns_on": "Whether the commands emphasize present needs or preparation for the final meeting, and what motive prompts worship.", "positions": [{"id": "29:17/q16/p1", "position": "Worship God alone, sincerely recognizing His worth and provision.", "reasons": "Muqātil specifies affirming oneness; al-Ṭabarī adds humility and recognition of blessing. {"id": "29:17/q17", "question": "Why and how should they thank God?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "29:17/q17/p1", "position": "Thank God alone for provision and all His blessings, through devotion and deeds.", "reasons": "Muqātil links gratitude to the living return after death; al-Ṭabarī to provision and blessing. {"id": "29:17/q28", "question": "What neighboring textual or recitational details are cited with this verse?", "turns_on": "The notes cite distinct neighboring reading details rather than competing analyses of one word.", "positions": [{"id": "29:17/q28/p1", "position": "A neighboring verb يبدا is read with softened rather than fully realized hamza.", "reasons": "Ibn Jinnī reports al-Zuhrī and argues true replacement would lead to yāʾ then alif, comparing Abū Zayd's poetic ملا for ملأ."}, {"id": "29:17/q28/p2", "position": "A connected recitation reads أوثانا مودةً with accusative tanwīn and بينكم accusative.", "reasons": "Al-Durr transmits this from ʿĀṣim together with his light reading of afkan."}]}

{"id": "29:29/q01", "question": "How is the opening أئنكم read?", "turns_on": "Whether the first corresponding clause asserts or asks, and how the interrogative hamza is realized; Abū ʿUbayd objects to two successive interrogatives and al-Naḥḥās answers him.", "positions": [{"id": "29:29/q01/p1", "position": "Both corresponding clauses are interrogative, with two articulated hamzas.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujāhid assigns this to Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza, and al-Kisāʾī; al-Naḥḥās calls it the Kufan reading.
